paragraphs: Say to him: tell us about God's saying to Israel (Deut 6:6): "And these words which I command thee this day shall be on thine heart…" and the rest of the pericope — what did He intend by this? He cannot but answer: He intended the commandments. We then put to him: it is [obligatory upon every Israelite] to write the Torah and read it all the days of his life, that he may learn and act on it. This corroborates what we said previously: learning and acting take place by reading and writing. Learning and acting are obligated on every man (Deut 5:1, "hear, O Israel … learn them, keep them, and do them"). The conclusion of these two premises is that writing and reading are obligated on all the people.

If they say: but if writing and reading are obligated on all, and the king is one of the people, why does Scripture single out the king with the special obligation (Deut 17:18)? Answer: Scripture did not say that the king is to write the Torah; it said, "he shall write for himself a copy (mishneh) of this Torah." It is possible that what is meant is a kind of commentary and interpretation — that is, the kind of knowledge of the modes and subtleties of the rulings that priests and Levites know but ordinary people do not. Since the king must judge, he needs to know the details of aḥkām (like Solomon, who manifests this expertise). The word mishneh itself signals "second" or "secondary" — i.e., a second-order knowledge that interprets the first. Mishneh in this verse refers to what follows from and complements the Torah-text: knowledge of its tafsīr and maʿānī. So we read of the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:14): "she dwelt in Jerusalem in the second quarter" — i.e., she sat there teaching people interpretation and meanings. ("Mishneh" of the city, "mishneh" of the Torah — by linguistic resonance.)[{2}]
As to what they have made of the narrative of the book that Hilkiah found — this does not indicate any of what they claim. […][{3}] ---
